title: No Teachers of Zen
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of self-compassion and embracing uncertainty in spiritual practice. It encourages individuals to take responsibility for their own growth and development, while also recognizing the value of guidance from a qualified teacher who embodies the principles of the tradition through their daily life and example. By letting go of ego and judgment, one can cultivate patience, forgiveness, and compassion, ultimately awakening the inherent goodness in themselves and others.

sentences.text: I really appreciated Tim's talk yesterday.

We're all getting the fruit of his study and training in the mindfulness tradition, and Flo was reminding me about how important it was when he was talking yesterday about self-compassion and how self-compassion works.
I'm probably getting it a little bit wrong, but I think what he was saying is that first you have to allow the difficult thought or feeling to be there.
Allow it to arise—the thought or feeling in you that maybe you don't like, or maybe you're ashamed of, or maybe you think it's immoral and completely unacceptable, but there it is.
You have to let it be there, and then you have to forgive yourself for it and be gentle with yourself.
Maybe develop a little sense of humor about it and realize that everybody has this; we all hate the people we love and we all want to beat everybody up and so on.
Normal.
So we have to forgive ourselves for this.
Anyway, that might not be exactly what he said, but you'll all have to listen to the talk online.
I recommend it.
Close enough?
Good.
Thank you.
I tend to garble almost everything, sorry.
But this is so important for our practice in our life to allow ourselves to be what we are—to allow whatever it is that wants to come and say, "What a crazy person I am."
It's okay.
It's alright.
I forgive myself.
And that's the way, that's the secret to living a life in which we no longer need to be pushed around all the time by our thoughts and feelings.
One's self is the greatest tyrant of all.
If we could only be free of ourselves a little bit, this would be great.
Then we could act with kindness and generosity more of the time.
Anyway, this was my favorite part of the talk and Flo's also.
But this morning I want to talk about something different from that.
I want to talk about teachers of Zen.

A topic I guess, you know, by now I've been yakking about this stuff for so long that I probably said about everything that could be said about anything you could talk about, so I probably talked about this many times before.
But it's not one of my themes, you know, one of my favorite topics.

The reason I'm talking about it today is because not long ago the editors of Buddha Dharma magazine were putting out an issue on Teachers of Zen, and they said to me, "Would you please write so many words about Teachers of Zen?"
They really like me because I write very fast and they don't have to edit me very much.
So when they're looking for something that they need fast, they say, "Will you write it?"
I say, "Sure," and I write it the next day.
So they asked me, "Would you write about Teachers of Zen?"
I said, "Well, sure."
And they said, "But one thing, be sure to be personal."
So I said, "OK, I'll be personal."
In fact, this issue of the Buddha Dharma magazine is out now, so I bet you some of you anyway have seen this, have seen this essay of mine on Teachers of Zen.
I'm sorry that I'm repeating it again, but hopefully it's worth repeating at least once.
So this is mine.
And actually, I don't know, I never read the magazine when it comes out, so I don't know what title they used, but the title that I sent them was *No Teachers of Zen*.
Is that the title that they used?
Yeah, *No Teachers of Zen*.
So one of my all-time favorite Zen stories is about this.
It's about Huang Bo, who was a great, powerful Chinese Zen teacher of the classical period.
Huang Bo strives into the Dharma hall and he says to the assembled monastics, "You people are all dreg slurpers.
If you go on like this, when will you ever see today?
Don't you know that in all of China there are no teachers of Zen?"

He says this, and so one intrepid monastic, you know, is not intimidated and comes forth and says to Huang Bo, "Well, yes, but what about all these people out there, for instance you, who set up Zen places and invite students and thousands of students come?
What do you call that?"
And Huang Bo says, "I didn't say there's no Zen, only that there are no teachers."

As an independent-minded person, some people might say, as people who know me well from childhood might say, not only independent-minded but absolutely stubborn person, I've always found this a very appealing story.
I have never been attracted to Zen masters or gurus of any sort.
Powerful, charismatic, spiritual guys have never done a thing for me.
One could doubt whether this actually does exist, this phenomenon of such people.
Maybe it does, maybe it doesn't, but anyway, it's something that has absolutely never interested me.
I have always assumed that I know what I need to know for my living, and that when I don't, I'll find out for myself somehow.
No wisdom, no experience that is not my own is ever going to be worthwhile for me.
So what would be the point, really, in spiritual teachers?
What benefit could anybody possibly gain from hanging around some supposed sage?
Even if such a person were transcendentally enlightened, fine, what good does that do me?
Good for them.
What good is that going to do for me?
So when I began my Zen study, my interest was, first and foremost, to learn how to do Zazen, so that I could find out firsthand what this Zen business is all about.
So I was perfectly happy to listen to talks and instructions that would help to orient me to the practice.
But the idea that somehow following a Zen teacher and hanging on his every word and deed, and his is the pronoun, because in the days when I began, all Zen teachers were male—not the case now.
There are more women Zen teachers than men, I'm pretty sure.
I haven't taken account, but I would guess, I'd be surprised if in the United States and Canada, there weren't more women Zen teachers than men.
Anyway, in those days, his every word and deed, how could that ever help me to become spiritually developed?
This seemed to me not only an unappealing prospect to hang around such a person, but also wrong.
It didn't make any sense.
And my idea was actually, on my own, quite similar to Huang Bo's.
I thought that there was real Zen, but that there were no teachers.

Now, I recognize, just as this student in the story implies, that yes, there are people who have credentials, and they set up shop, and they welcome students, because yes, we need a structure, and we need a place to practice.
So I get that, and I got that then, but a teacher can't teach you.
Your practice really is completely up to you.
In other words, good old American individualism.
And I believed it so much, that I had no interest whatsoever in encountering teachers.
So at the time that I began practicing, there were lots of really great Asian teachers who came through the San Francisco Bay area where I was living, and now most of them are dead.
Now, there are no great teachers alive anymore.
But in those days there were.
I mean, there's a few.
There's Thich Nhat Hanh and Dalai Lama.
But they're impossible to talk to anyway, because so many millions of people around them.
Somebody said, like the Dalai Lama was recently in the Bay area, and somebody went to hear him talk, and I said, "Well, how was it?"
And they said, "Well, the Dalai Lama was around this big, on this grand stage, way, way over there, surrounded by people.
I wasn't even sure whether it was him or some imposter, you know?"
But in those days, you could actually, I mean, actually you could, you know, be close and talk to them and be with them and so on.
But I was totally uninterested in this.
I first came to the San Francisco Zen Center in the spring of 1970, and in the spring of 1970, Suzuki Roshi was still alive.
But I made absolutely no effort to ever speak to him, meet him, hear him talk.
When I saw notice of his funeral on the board, I thought, "Why would I go to that?"

When I saw notice that his successor, the first American Zen master to be installed as an abbot of a major temple, was going to have his installation ceremony, I thought, "Why would I ever want to go to that?"
I never went to any of these things.
Now that I look back on it, I think, "Damn, you know, what was wrong with me?"
I knew it.
Great opportunities.
I would have been so great, you know, but that's just the way I was, you know, at the time.
So hearing this, you might think, you know, well, he was a very rebellious Zen student.
But that's not right.
I wasn't rebellious.
I had no problem respecting the teachers that were in front of me, and I would listen to their talks.
And, you know, you were supposed to go to interviews, so I went to, you know, to Dokusan, and I went to Dokusan.
That was fine.
So I had no problem with it.

Because I think that when you have a need to rebel, challenge, or deny teachers, I think what usually is going on is you are setting up a teacher in your mind who does fulfill the ideal requirements that the teacher in front of you is failing to fulfill.
So I think if you feel compelled to rebel, it's probably because of that.
Probably because you actually do believe in an idealized, almighty, spiritual master, and you're disappointed that this person in front of you is not quite measuring up.
But I didn't believe in such a thing in the first place.
So I didn't need to rebel, and I had no problem with the Zen Center and its leadership.
I was there to study Zen.
I had my own reasons for wanting to do that.
And since the teachers were in charge, I would cooperate.
Why not?
But whatever benefit or understanding I got out of it was going to be my own affair.
No one else could give it to me or even lead me to it.
So I'm telling you all this because the editors of the Buddha Dharma said, "Be personal."
And this was actually how I felt at the time.
Not that I agree with myself now, but at the time that was my feeling.
The absolute furthest thing from my mind was that I would ever be a Zen teacher myself.
This was completely, not only didn't I ever think of it, but if anybody ever said it to me, I would say, "Are you crazy?
It's the last thing that I want to want to do."
My idea was, very simply, that I would get what I needed from the practice and then would go forth with my vague life as a poet, and I would survive somehow.
In those days, we all believed that we would survive somehow.

My wife Cathy and I were ordained as Zen priests together on January the 6th, 1980, because our teacher required us to either do that and continue to practice full time at the center, which we had been doing since about 1976, or move on and get a life.
Because by then we already had two children.
So our teacher basically said, "You either get ordained as a priest or go figure out what to do."
And I was not ready for that.
So I said, "Well, this is the lesser of two evils."
And so we did ordain, and my wife Cathy was much more ready for this step than I was, but she helped me along and I managed to get through the ceremony and have my head shaved and all that.
I used to have quite nice hair, actually, big, a lot of curls and everything.
I don't know what would happen now if I had long hair so long ago.
When in 1988 my teacher offered me Shiho, Dharma Transmission, which is a full ordination as a Soto Zen priest, I was shocked and surprised by this offer.
Because in those days in American Zen, Shiho was extremely rare, though in Japan at the time and now, it's not rare at all.
Most young men whose daddies are priests and have temples receive Shiho in their 20s after they spend a little time at the monastery.
They go home and they receive Shiho in preparation for taking over someday as abbot in the family temple.
So it was very common in Japan, but in America it was not common at all.
We all assumed that only deeply enlightened people would receive Shiho, which is why I was so surprised.
Why would they ask me to do this?
But I thought, "Well, let's see what happens."
I went ahead with the process and I became officially a Zen teacher, a role I found at first somewhat absurd and disturbing because I was so ill-prepared for it and not very well suited for it.
Eventually though, with Huang Bo in mind, I came to be able to accept the social designation, Zen priest or Zen teacher.
And ever since then, I have done the best I could to try to help people to practice.
When you think about it more though, there's more to this, *No Teachers of Zen*, than meets the eye at first.
I still do believe that students are responsible for their own practice and their own awakening.
I still do believe that no one can communicate a truth worth knowing.
That the only worthwhile truth is the one that you find uniquely for your own life.
On the other hand, I now know that Zen is not American individualism.
Zen is not lone ranger practice.
And I now know that Zen teachers really are important to the practice, as the lore of the tradition certainly indicates and as experience proves.
Yes, on the one hand, there are no teachers of Zen because Zen isn't teachable subject matter or a learned skill.

Although there are plenty of things you can learn, like how to sit for instance, how to walk into a Zen though, how to bow to your cushion, how to strike a bell at the right time in the right way, how to chant, some acquaintance with liturgy, some acquaintance with the tradition's teachings.
So yes, there are things you can learn.
But it's also clear that the actual Zen itself, while it's not exactly something other than these things, isn't also exactly the same as these things either.
It's a lot more slippery or ineffable than that.
And you know, when you take just five minutes, look at Zen literature, makes that pretty clear.
*The Heart Sutra teaches us all dharmas are empty.
Zen is empty.
It's empty of a specific content, empty of specific doctrine, empty of specific form or faith that can be codified and defined, even though it has all these things.* It's something more than that.
So what is it that one would teach?
But on the other hand, yes, there are Zen teachers because Zen practice is not nothing.
Real transformation occurs through the practice, as many of you in the room will attest through your own lives.
So there's something to this, somehow.
And Zen teachers cannot show you how to affect this transformation, and they can't cause it to happen in you.
And they're not masters of it, because no one could be a master of this indefinable, empty, difficult to understand feeling for living.
And yet, Zen teachers play an essential role.
In the ordinary educational model, there are teachers who teach, and these are different from the students who learn.
There's a subject matter.
There are standards of knowledge.
There's an educational institution which contains and certifies the educational process.
In some ways, Zen institutions and Zen life might look like this, but in fact Zen is not an educational proposition.
It's a transformational process in which both teachers and students must fully engage, and each one plays his or her proper role in the process.
And it's the process itself and its entirety that affects the transformation.
You can think of it as a machine with many moving parts that interact in a complex system.
Each part affects every other part, and all the parts have to be in working order in order for the machine to function.
In a machine, you don't say, "Well, this part of the machine teaches that part of the machine, which learns."
No, the whole machine turns, and when you run it for a while, it accomplishes something.

A product is produced, in this case a seasoned Zen practitioner, who will embody in his or her own absolutely unique way the values, commitments, and mostly the feeling of, the vision of a life of practice.
People teach, not by teaching, but by living their lives.
So it's just like Huang Bo says, there is Zen for sure, but strictly speaking, no teachers.
Although, yes, that's right, the machine will not turn unless all the parts are there and functioning fully, each one in good working order in its proper place.
Right?
Machine got a part missing, doesn't work.
Got to get the right part, it has to be in good shape, in the right spot.
So the teacher, who's not actually teaching anything, has a place, a part in the system.
In order for the teacher to take his or her place in that process, I would say that certain capacities would be really helpful.
And the first capacity would be faith in the practice.
And I don't mean just enthusiastic faith, but faith grounded in real experience over time.
Faith that's not only spoken of with brilliant speeches, but faith that's demonstrated in action every day.
And experience in the lived reality of the practice is the source of this kind of faith.
You don't get it from the sky or from some visitation.

You get it day by day by day through lived experience in the practice, until you come to a time in your life when you know for sure, to the very bones, no doubt about it, that practice is the truest way to live a human life.
And practice here doesn't just mean formal practice that happens in temples and meditation halls.
It means understanding and living a human life among others, for and with others.
Meditation practice is pretty new in Western culture, and naturally, we've enthusiastically overemphasized meditation practice.
We've romanticized all the unusual mystical type experiences that intensive meditation can produce, but all these things are simply a matter of course.
I think they're among the least important things for teachers to have experienced, though any Zen teacher who has practiced for a while will have experienced many, many things in meditation.
You sit there long enough, and pretty much everything and anything is bound to occur eventually.
But it isn't those experiences that matter as much as the folding of those experiences into a whole life and a whole view.
Even this depth of faith, though I think it's essential, is not sufficient.
Ideally, a Zen teacher would also be willing and able to share life completely with others, and this is not so easy.

This takes a wide and deep acceptance—acceptance of and even an interest in the many wily and wild manifestations of the human heart, which will arise eventually in the course of practice over time, practice with people for a while.

And you will bear witness at close range to births, deaths, marriages, divorces, love affairs, broken love affairs, enlightenment experiences, endless, endless tears, tragic, horrible illnesses, angry feuds, breaches, collapses, and surprises of every sort you can imagine.
A Zen teacher will eventually live through all of this with others; he will eventually live through almost everything human beings perpetrate.
So he or she better have long patience and deep forbearance, wide forgiveness, and a healthy sense of the immense tragedy and beauty of our human life.

The more the teacher of Zen has an idea of Zen that students must conform to, and sometimes such ideas are communicated without ever saying any words, the more the teacher has such an idea, the more will everyone, perhaps especially including the teacher, suffer.
If not at first, then later, as people who were initially really inspired by that wonderful idea of Zen, will eventually feel themselves oppressed by it or even betrayed by it.

No doubt there are many other important skills people would like their Zen teachers to have, but I think that if they would have deep faith and a willingness to share their lives honestly with others, that would be pretty good.
Those, to me, are the most important things.
However, having said that, I also would note that I have seen Zen teachers who seem seriously lacking in both these things, who have nevertheless been able to benefit others.
So there are no absolute rules at all in Zen or in human life.
Zen practice is dialogical; it's interactive.
Compared to other forms of Buddhism, the characteristic of Zen, as they sometimes say in Japan or Korea, is together practice, as we're experiencing this weekend.
We all eat together, we start at the same time, we end at the same time.
We don't all go our own walks; we walk together in single file, evenly spaced.
We don't all go off to our own huts to meditate; we start every period of meditation together and we end it together.
And, as I've often said, when you think about the characteristic form of Zen literature, it's not scriptures and speeches.
It's dialogues, exchanges, often brief exchanges, sometimes using very few words, sometimes none, between people, practicing together side by side.

And one of the most characteristic of all Zen practices is Dokusan, which is a meeting, a face-to-face meeting, which is viewed not as reporting in or asking technical questions, although one could report in or ask technical questions, but the idea of Dokusan is not that.
The idea of Dokusan is face-to-face Dharma encounter, a chance to deeply meet oneself through meeting another.
So given this radically together style, it's clear that a Zen teacher has got to be ready all the time to let go of his life and be ready to enter the life of another.
This deep mutuality is the essence of Zen practice, and it's been wonderful, wonderful training for a stubborn person like me.
Boy, did it help me.
I might not be doing that well, but I shudder to think of how I would be doing if I hadn't done all of this.
It's really helped me a lot, but it took a long time for me to be ready for this, or even know that this was what it was about.
I had no idea.
Very soon after my Shiho ceremony, I had a personal crisis.
I read a line in some book by Thich Nhat Hanh, something to the effect of, if you cannot find a true teacher, it's better not to study at all.
I thought, true teacher?
I was immediately tangled up in the net of my unacknowledged preconceptions about Zen teachers.
It was really upsetting to me because it seemed to imply that there was some exalted state, called a true teacher, and I knew that wasn't me.
And yet, here I was, one of, I don't know how many people there were at the time with Shiho in the United States, but maybe ten, I don't know, some really small number.
What in the world did I think I was doing?
So it took me a few uncomfortable years to finally catch up to Thich Nhat Hanh and get him to sit down and talk to me about this.
I was talking to Wendy Johnson the other day; I gave this talk at Green Gulch, and Wendy came to it, and she said, I remember when you had that conversation with Thich Nhat Hanh.
She was sitting there at the table because I didn't, I wasn't private.
It was like we were sitting at a table with other people.
It was the only way I could get a hold of him.
He's such a man.
But I asked him about this, and he said something like, don't worry, don't worry.
We're all just helping each other.
The one-day person helps the person who just walked in the door.
The five-year person helps the one-year person.
We're all helping each other, according to our experience.
After that, I felt much better.
I could do that.
Still, it took some years, maybe ten or so, to feel comfortable in the teacher's seat.
And maybe that's the thing about being a so-called Zen teacher, is just to be able to sit in the seat and feel comfortable in your robe, in your body, in that seat.
For a few years, I was unconsciously caught by the idea that I was supposed to be someone that others expected me to be.
So naturally, I was straining a bit to be that person, but eventually I realized that there was no one in particular I needed to be.
As you might know, a Zen talk like the one I'm giving now is not conceived of as a learned lecture on Zen.
The technical term for it in Japanese translates as presenting the shout.
So that's what a Zen talk is.
It's not a talk about Zen or Buddhism; it's just presenting the shout.
In other words, expressing the teaching simply by speaking in your own voice, being the person you are.
I have always appreciated the fact that when you give a Zen talk, as I did today, you begin by making three prostrations to the Buddha.
You do it before the talk, and you do it after the talk.
These bows are meant to indicate that it's not you giving the talk; it's the Buddha using your body and voice to express himself.

When you bow, you are praying to the Buddha, please help me to do a good job channeling you in the faith that whatever you're going to say, whether it's right or wrong, will be of some use if you are sincere and try your best.
After some years I came to see that this was so in general about anything that I did as a Zen teacher.
If I was honest, if I tried my best, I'm not being arrogant, not taking it for granted, but really trying.
If I followed precepts, if I didn't try to pretend to be anyone, then everything would be okay.
This sounds very simple-minded, I admit, and in fact, it is simple-minded, but it's not actually so easy to do.
And anyway, what do I mean by everything would be okay?
Everything will go well?
No.
Everything will not go well.
As a matter of fact, if there's one thing you could guarantee, it's that things will not always go well; things will go wrong.
So maybe, as I'm thinking about it, another capacity a Zen teacher should develop is resilience and breadth of view that will enable her to live with the fact that she is guaranteed to fail.
Or at least, this is my personal experience.

Occupying the teacher gear in the whirling Zen machine requires that you receive all ensundry with an open heart and the willingness and the stamina to take full responsibility for each and every relationship you enter.
Which means that you care and that you try your best to help.
People come to Zen practice as they come to any spiritual practice and perhaps as they come to any human endeavor with lots of human need.
They come with trust.
They come with mistrust.
They come with tremendous wounds and hidden expectations.
And of course, the Zen teacher, who is after all only a person, a human being, is inevitably going to disappoint a fair number of them.
If you're lucky, they'll be disappointed on the first day.
If you're less lucky, it may take them decades to be disappointed in you because you're going to misunderstand them and they're going to misunderstand you.
You're going to say and do things that are hurtful without ever intending to.
Trying to straighten somebody out, which I have come to realize is a highly dubious proposition, you will completely botch the job.
Instead, you will reinforce by a factor of ten the behavior that you were trying to clear up.
Students who have practiced faithfully with you for many years will finally realize that it's all been a mistake, and they will leave.
When they do, they'll create enormous confusion in the sangha.
Like, what happened there?
What's wrong?
Your public words and actions will, in being variously understood, create confusion and dissonance and dissension among people.
They'll act out their confusion in sometimes painful ways.
You will have all kinds of complicated and contradictory feelings about people who come to practice you.
You will love them.
You will worry about them desperately.
You will have hopes for them.
You will sometimes dread them.
You will watch with your mouth wide open as they make horrible mistakes that you are totally unable to prevent.
You will watch with even more amazement as they manipulate you and set you up for all sorts of falls which you can't prevent.

In the end, you'll come to realize that you cannot help them at all, and there's nothing else that you can do but watch them suffer the sufferings that they need to suffer, or watch them make you suffer and maintain your composure even so.
Anyway, this is all just a personal confession of things that have actually happened to me.
Maybe nobody else who teaches Zen has this problem.
It could just be me, but I doubt it.
I think it resonates with me.
When I gave this talk, there were other Zen teachers in the room who were smiling and laughing at a lot of it, so I figured I might not be the only one, but I admit that it's possible, it's just me.
So now there are lots of Zen teachers.
I remember years ago writing, we won't understand what Zen is or Zen teachers are until every street corner has a Zen teacher.
Now we're getting there.
Almost now every street corner has a Zen teacher.
And I speak to a lot of Zen teachers and we talk shop.
A lot of them are trying to get better at being Zen teachers.
They're trying to see how they make mistakes.
They're trying to figure out how to correct their mistakes.

Some of them try to get training of some kind, like psychological training or training in how to run a temple or things like that so that they can understand how to do these things and avoid some of the pitfalls.
It's been very helpful now that there are so many Zen teachers, that Zen teachers can talk to each other and there are associations and meetings, and that really helps a lot.
It's made a big difference in the American Zen tradition.
But I confess that I believe that in the end, Zen teachers can no more learn than they can teach because every situation and every person is completely unique.
You can't say, when a person like this comes along, do this.
When this situation happens, do that, because this situation never happened before, and this person never came along before.
Even if that person did come along before, they never came along today before, because a person that you know for ten years is not the same today as they've been.
So you can't really learn how to do it.
All you can do is respond to that person at that time, to that situation at that time, in a unique way, suitable to that moment, the best you can.
I myself have come to completely and always trust my responses.
I know that it could be the wrong response in that moment, nevertheless, I trust my response.
And if it's wrong, I'll find out and I'll try to correct.
But in the end, I trust my response because I know that I will never get it right.
There is no such thing as getting it right.
I've seen more than once that getting it absolutely wrong sometimes is the best thing.
It helps a lot more and it's better.
So in the end, it is true, everything does turn out okay, but not in the way we think.

When you really trust the process of practice more than you trust your limited self, the limited sangha, or what happens in the short run, you realize that the magic of the practice is far stronger than you ever imagined.
It's not limited to what you or anyone else says or does.
It's not limited to meditation or what takes place in meditation halls or on temple grounds.
I've seen it happen now; it's been enough years, but I've seen it happen many times.

That after five years, ten years, twenty years or more, maybe after leaving your presence and place of practice in a huff, in disgust or not, students' lives miraculously turn around because of unexpected circumstances that Buddha somehow placed in the middle of their lives long after they left your presence.
The perfect priest you thought you were ordaining turns out completely unbeknownst to you to need to completely fall apart.
Leave you and go through tragic ups and downs for decades before she finally will emerge as the Buddha you always knew she was.
The wreck of a human being who was so disruptive and annoying and completely hopeless comes back to visit you decades later shining with love and wisdom.
That crazy mixed-up young woman who seemed headed for certain doom returns with her three lovely children, grateful for the practice, she seemed to have resisted so mightily at the time.
These things have happened.
And when you see them happen over and over again, you do finally come around to completely trusting the practice and trusting life.
This helps you to trust yourself and the basic goodness of everyone you will ever practice with and everyone you will ever meet.
And it turns out that that is the secret ingredient in teaching Zen: the brilliant spark of human goodness in each and every person.
Practice awakens it, and once it's awakened, it does the rest on its own, eventually.
You, the teacher, just have to be willing to be there and be surprised.
So, this is a lot more than, meditate, breathe, calm down, be more mindful.
Yes, please breathe.
I really recommend it.
I think you should do it all your life.
That's why I always figure, everybody's practicing with us, right?
Anybody who's breathing, they're doing the practice.
So, yes, I recommend, please breathe.
Please pay attention, be mindful.
Please practice.
Please help one another.
But this life that we're living, this practice that we're doing, it has no boundaries.
It's bigger than any of us can know.
To know that much, that it is that way, is really beautiful, really wonderful.
I can't imagine a more wonderful human life than this, to know that we're all doing this together, that we're all going somewhere, that we're all going to get there.
No matter how much we stumble and fall down and scrape our knee, we're all getting there.
